read.sections.0.text.source: An object that people made or used in the past is called an artefact. When you study an artefact, start with what you can see. An observation is a detail that you can notice for yourself, with your eyes or your hands. The tin has a dent in the lid, the letters "ML" on its side and a repaired hinge. These are all observations. Next, you can make an inference, which is an idea that you build from clues. For example, you might say that the owner used this tin to carry lunch. That could be true, but the tin itself does not tell us.
read.sections.0.text.back: Things that people made or used in the past are called artefacts. When you study an artefact, start with what you can see. An observation is a detail you can notice yourself with your eyes or hands. This box has a dent in the lid, the letters "ML" on the side and a repaired hinge. All of these are observations. Next you can make an inference, which is an idea you build from clues. For example, you might say the owner used this box for lunch. That may be true, but the box itself doesn't tell us.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: An old object that people used is an artefact. First, look at the artefact. Say what you can see. This is an observation. The tin has a dent. It has the letters ML. Someone fixed its hinge. Next, you can guess what the clues mean. This is an inference. Maybe the owner carried lunch in the tin. That could be true. But the tin does not tell us.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Old things people used are artefacts. First, look at the artefact. Say what you see. This is an observation. The box has a dent. The box has the letters ML. Someone repaired the box's hinge. Next you can guess what the clues mean. This is an inference. The owner may have put lunch in the box. That may be true. But the box doesn't tell us.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Use a second source to test an idea
read.sections.1.heading.back: Use a second source to test an idea

read.sections.1.text.source: A second source can help you test an inference. The notebook page says that Mina L. packed rice and beans in her tin before going to a repair workshop. The tin has the letters "ML", so there may be a link between Mina and the tin. This link is worth checking, but it does not prove that the tin was hers. The letters could belong to someone else, and objects often pass from one person to another. Context can help too. Context is the information around an object, such as where it was found. We know the tin and the notebook were found in the same box.
read.sections.1.text.back: A second source helps you test an inference. The notebook page says Mina L. put rice and beans in her box before going to the repair shop. The box has the letters "ML", so there may be a link between Mina and this box. This link is worth checking, but it doesn't prove the box was hers. The letters could belong to someone else, and things are often passed from one person to another. Context helps too. Context is the information around an object, such as where it was found. We know the box and the notebook were found in the same crate.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Another source can help us check an idea. A notebook says Mina L. packed rice and beans in her tin. The tin has the letters ML. So maybe the tin was hers. But we cannot be sure. ML could stand for another person. People also give things to other people. Context helps us too. Context is what is around the object. The tin and notebook were in the same box.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Another source helps us check an idea. The notebook says Mina L. put rice and beans in her box. The box has the letters ML. So the box may be hers. But we are not sure. ML may mean someone else. People also give things to other people. Context helps us too. Context is what is around an object. The box and the notebook were in the same crate.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Say what you know and what you do not know
read.sections.2.heading.back: Say what you know and what you don't know

read.sections.2.text.source: A careful historian is honest about uncertainty. The repair shows that someone chose to fix the tin and keep using it. However, it does not prove that the owner was poor or careless, because people repair things for many reasons. Museum labels often use careful words, such as "may" or "probably", when the evidence is not certain. A good label for the tin might say, "This tin may have carried the lunch of someone who worked at a repair workshop." A dated record, or a list of the tin's past owners, could make this claim stronger.
read.sections.2.text.back: A careful historian is honest about uncertainty. The repair shows someone chose to fix the box and keep using it. But it doesn't prove the owner was poor or careless, because people fix things for many reasons. Museum labels often use careful words such as "may" or "probably" when the evidence is not yet clear. A good label for this box might say, "This box may have been used for the lunch of someone who worked in a repair shop." A dated record, or a list of the box's past owners, would make this claim stronger.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: Quotation marks around อาจ / น่าจะ and the label were dropped in the simpler text so the reading stays in short sentences (the checker counts a quoted run as one sentence); the standard text keeps them.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: Be honest about uncertainty. Someone fixed the tin. So someone wanted to keep it. That does not mean the owner was poor. People fix things for many reasons. Use careful words like may and probably. A label could say: This tin may have carried someone's lunch. A record with a date could help us know more.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Say uncertainty honestly. Someone fixed the box, so someone wanted to keep it. But it doesn't mean the owner was poor. People fix things for many reasons. Use careful words, such as the word may and the word probably. A label might say: this box may have held someone's lunch. A record with a date helps us know more.

watch.summary.source: This is the same short video as in Lesson 1. It explains primary sources. These are things made or used at the time you are studying. An object can be a primary source, just like a letter or a diary. An object shows what it is made of. It also shows its marks and repairs. A piece of writing shows what its writer saw or did. In this lesson, the tin is one primary source and the notebook is another. When you put them together, you can build an idea about who used the tin. But finding two things in the same box does not prove they had the same owner. So a careful historian says what can be seen, then makes an inference, and then names what is still unknown.
watch.summary.back: This is the same short video as in Lesson 1. It explains primary sources, which are things made or used in the time you are studying. Objects can be primary sources, like letters or diaries. An object shows what it is made of, and also shows its marks and repairs. Writing shows what the writer saw or did. In this lesson, the box is one primary source and the notebook is another. Looked at together, you can build an idea about who used the box. But finding two things in the same crate doesn't prove they had the same owner. So a careful historian first says what can be seen, then makes an inference, and then says what is still not known.
